unit.subject: English
unit.unitOverview: Unit 4 explores myths and legends, the timeless tales families have retold for centuries. You will read an information text about the two forms, the legend of the Whispering Dunes, and the three-part desert adventure "The Hasty Route". You will study twenty-five describing words, from hasty and reluctant to justifiable and prosperous, in four groups. The language focus is the defining relative clause, supported by present continuous for arranged plans, comparative adjectives, opposites and verb-noun collocations, and the unit closes with you writing an original legend of your own.
unit.learningPath: Preview the goals and the four vocabulary groups. Read the information text, the legend and the three parts of "The Hasty Route". Answer the comprehension questions with evidence from the passage named. Work through the six grammar lessons on defining relative clauses and the Grade 5 editing focus. Practise the speaking tasks, complete the vocabulary activities, draft and revise your own legend, then finish with the quiz and self-assessment.

readings.title: Myths and Legends: What Makes a Tale Timeless
readings.theme: Myths, legends and the tales that outlast us
readings.setting: A Grade 5 classroom studying classic tales
readings.passageScript:
Myths and legends are the timeless tales that families have told for hundreds, and sometimes thousands, of years.
A myth is an ancient story that explains something in nature. It might explain why the sun rises, why the sea tastes salty, or why thunder rolls across the sky. Myths usually include gods, spirits or other beings with powers no person could have. A myth is not based on fact, and it is set in a vague, timeless past that begins "Long, long ago".
A legend works differently. A legend grows out of a real place, a real period of history, or a person who may once have lived. Storytellers then add unlikely details until the tale stands far larger than the truth. A legend usually follows a hero or heroine on a quest, and it ends by teaching something about courage, patience or loyalty.
The two kinds of tale share a great deal. Both travelled by oral tradition, which means people spoke them aloud long before anyone wrote them down. Both open with a familiar phrase such as "In ancient times". Both carry larger-than-life characters, vivid description, and a moral for the listener.
So when you meet a classic tale, ask two questions. Does it explain a natural event? If it does, the tale is probably a myth. Does it follow a human hero on a quest? If it does, the tale is probably a legend. Some remarkable stories manage both at once.

readings.title: The Legend of the Whispering Dunes
readings.theme: Myths, legends and the tales that outlast us
readings.setting: A village on the edge of a great desert, long ago
readings.passageScript:
Long ago, on the edge of a great desert, there lived a girl named Zara who was known for her remarkable memory. The elders said she could repeat every word of every story she had ever heard.
One dry season the wells that supplied the village began to fail, one after another. The phenomenon puzzled everyone. Where had the water gone?
Zara remembered a legend her grandmother had told her. It spoke of a hidden spring beneath the Whispering Dunes, sand hills that hummed a low note when the wind crossed them. The spring, the story said, would show itself only to a patient and reliable traveller. Only someone who followed the sound without making a hasty choice would ever find it.
"I will go," Zara told the elders. Her cousin walked beside her, anxious but brave, and together they set off across the burning sand.
By the second day the heat was dreadful. Her cousin pointed at a pool of blue water shimmering far ahead. "Let us run to it!" he cried. Zara shook her head. "That is a mirage, a trick of the light. The spring we seek is the one that whispers. Listen."
On the third morning Zara heard a faint hum. She walked slowly, placing each foot with care, until she reached a hollow between two tall dunes. The sand there was dark and damp. She knelt, dug with her hands, and cool water bubbled up between her fingers.
The village was grateful beyond words, and the elders called Zara's deed honourable. They added one line to the old legend: "A reliable heart that listens will always find what a hasty foot runs past."

readings.title: The Hasty Route, part 1
readings.theme: Myths, legends and the tales that outlast us
readings.setting: The Adrar Plateau in the deserts of Mauritania
readings.passageScript:
In the hot, golden deserts of Mauritania, a team of young explorers prepared for a journey across the Adrar Plateau. They were led by ten-year-old Amal, a careful thinker, and by her cousin Noah, who was brave but often made hasty decisions.
"This is a map of the route we are taking," Amal said, spreading it across a flat rock. "We are documenting sand-dwelling animals and ancient wells this week. We are also testing the new water-purifying backpack."
Noah waved a hand. "We should skip the first stop. It is slower. Let us head straight to the mountain site."
Amal looked at him steadily. "That is a reasonable idea if the weather holds. But the guide said sandstorms are common today."
"I am not reluctant to take risks," Noah said forcefully. "Let us move quickly before it gets hotter."
The group hesitated. Amal studied the clouds. "We are documenting the full route tomorrow. Today's walk is only a check."
By noon the sun stood high and the wind picked up. The team reached a small ridge where the air grew cooler and surprisingly pleasant. They ate lunch under a large rock, sharing stories and laughing.
"I am grateful we packed shade cloths," said Leo, the youngest walker in the team.
"I am grateful I listened to Amal," added Daniel. "This side of the ridge is cooler than the other."
Then a loud sound rolled across the dunes: wind, fast and heavy.
"It is a sandstorm!" shouted Noah.
They scrambled to cover the supplies and crouched under the cloths while the sand hit them like needles.
"This is dreadful," coughed Leo. "We should have stayed at camp."
"We simply need to wait it out," said Amal.

readings.title: The Hasty Route, part 2
readings.theme: Myths, legends and the tales that outlast us
readings.setting: The dunes and the ancient well beyond the ridge
readings.passageScript:
After twenty minutes the wind died away. The world around them looked different. Their footprints had vanished, and so had the spare map, blown somewhere across the dunes.
"We are off-track now," said Noah, brushing sand from his pack. "Perhaps this is my fault."
Amal did not blame him. "It was a justifiable mistake. You wanted to save time. Now we need to be reliable and put it right."
They checked the compass, followed the shadows, and rejoined the path within the hour. Ahead of them stood a round stone structure.
"What is that?" Leo asked.
Amal smiled. "It is an ancient well. We have found it!"
The group approached slowly. Around the rim lay carvings of animals, carvings of maps, and a mysterious pattern that glittered faintly in the sun.
Amal knelt down. "These are symbols cut by early traders. This is a remarkable find."
"Do you think they camped here?" Noah asked.
"Possibly," Amal said. "There is evidence of firestones and crushed herbs. The well may once have been a stop on a trading route."
Daniel leaned forward. "We should collect a soil sample. That could help us prove how old the well is."
Leo scribbled notes. "This is becoming more than a school project. It feels like a real expedition."
Amal grinned. "It is. And we are documenting history."
The team took photographs, sketched the site, and filtered a little of the well water.
"Let us label this place Desert Point 4," said Amal. "We are recording it properly tomorrow, right after we revisit the southern path."
"We are going back?" Leo asked, looking curious.
"Yes," Amal said. "We are presenting the full trail report to the science club next week."
"I am still feeling a little anxious about the return walk," Noah admitted.
"It will be more pleasant now that we know the path," said Daniel. "I will lead that part."

readings.title: The Hasty Route, part 3
readings.theme: Myths, legends and the tales that outlast us
readings.setting: The expedition camp and the school science fair
readings.passageScript:
Back at camp that night the team compared the two paths by lamplight. Amal wrote in the log:
"Route A was more comfortable, less dangerous, and full of ancient clues. Route B was shorter, but hotter and riskier. The dreadful wind made it miserable."
Noah added a line of his own:
"I was too forceful in my choice. Amal's slower plan was wiser. Her idea to explore carefully led to a profitable find."
Later, around the fire, they sipped warm tea. Leo asked, "Do you think we will be chosen to present at the regional fair?"
"I think we have a good chance," Amal replied. "Our site is unique, and we worked well together."
Noah nodded. "We disagreed, but we kept moving. That is what made it honourable."
The next day the team began preparing their presentation.
"We are writing about the explorers who found Desert Point 4," said Amal.
"And about the decisions that taught them patience," Noah added.
They printed photographs, drew diagrams, and annotated the map. Their report contained one sentence Amal was proud of:
"The storm that delayed us led to a well which had never been recorded before."
At the school fair a judge asked, "Was the storm a mistake?"
"No," Amal replied. "It was part of the journey."
"And would you do it again?" the judge asked.
"Only with this team," she said, smiling. "They are the most faithful, most dutiful, most honourable crew imaginable."

grammar.title: What a Defining Relative Clause Does
grammar.explanation: A defining relative clause is a group of words that tells the reader exactly which person, place or thing the sentence means. Remove it and the sentence loses the information the reader needs.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Pattern: noun + who / which / that + essential information.
The explorer who made the remarkable discovery shared it with her team.
Use who for people: The girl who found the spring saved the village.
Use which for things: The spring which lay beneath the dunes was hidden for centuries.
Use that for people or things: The path that Amal followed was safe.
Strip the clause away and "The explorer shared it with her team" leaves the reader asking which explorer.
grammar.commonMistake: Learners often keep the bare noun and drop the clause, so the reader cannot tell which explorer, spring or path is meant.
grammar.memoryTip: Cover the clause with one finger. If the sentence stops making sense, the clause is defining and has to stay.
grammar.practice:
Part A: Underline the defining relative clause in five sentences taken from "The Hasty Route". Part B: Beside each one, write the noun the clause describes. Part C: For two of them, explain in one sentence what the reader would lose if the clause disappeared.

Answer key (self-check): Part A/B – five defining relative clauses from “The Hasty Route” and the noun each one describes: (1) “The team reached a small ridge where the air grew cooler and surprisingly pleasant” – the clause describes ridge. (2) “...a mysterious pattern that glittered faintly in the sun” – the clause describes pattern. (3) “We are writing about the explorers who found Desert Point 4” – the clause describes explorers. (4) “...the decisions that taught them patience” – the clause describes decisions. (5) “The storm that delayed us led to a well which had never been recorded before” – two clauses here: “that delayed us” describes storm and “which had never been recorded before” describes well. Part C (model explanations for two): remove “who found Desert Point 4” and the reader no longer knows which explorers are meant; remove “that delayed us” and the reader loses the link between the storm and the well that was found afterwards.

grammar.title: Building a Defining Relative Clause in Four Steps
grammar.explanation: Building the clause takes four moves: name the noun, choose the pronoun, add the essential detail, then park the clause immediately after the noun.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Step 1, name the noun: the explorer.
Step 2, choose the pronoun: who for people, which for things, that for either.
Step 3, add the essential information: who made the discovery.
Step 4, place the clause straight after the noun: The explorer who made the discovery shared the map.
More models: The teacher who told us the legend was very animated. The well which they found had carvings on its stones. The children that listened carefully remembered the whole story.
grammar.commonMistake: The clause sometimes ends up at the end of the sentence, far from its noun, so it appears to describe the wrong thing.
grammar.memoryTip: Think of three keys: who opens the people door, which opens the things door, and that is the master key that fits both.
grammar.practice:
Part A: Fill each gap with who, which or that. The teacher ___ told us the legend. The book ___ I borrowed from the library. The traveller ___ crossed the desert alone. The well ___ they found. The children ___ listened carefully. The storm ___ delayed us. Part B: Write three sentences of your own, using each pronoun once. Part C: Circle the noun that each of your clauses describes.

Answer key (self-check): Part A – The teacher who told us the legend. The book which I borrowed from the library. The traveller who crossed the desert alone. The well which they found. The children who listened carefully. The storm which delayed us. (who = people, which = things; “that” is also grammatically correct in every blank.) Parts B and C ask for sentences “of your own,” so there is no single fixed answer – self-check instead by confirming you used who for a person, which for a thing, and that for either, with the clause placed right after the noun it describes, for example: “The girl who won the race trained every day” (who → girl); “The trophy which she won is silver” (which → trophy); “The coach that trained her was strict” (that → coach).

grammar.title: Folding Two Sentences into One
grammar.explanation: Two short sentences about the same noun can be folded into one, with the second sentence turning into the relative clause.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
The dog barked all night. It belongs to my neighbour. The dog that barked all night belongs to my neighbour.
The teacher told us the story. She is very kind. The teacher who told us the story is very kind.
The girl saved the village. She found the hidden spring. The girl who found the hidden spring saved the village.
The map was old. It showed the route to the dunes. The map that showed the route to the dunes was old.
The legend teaches patience. It has been told for generations. The legend that has been told for generations teaches patience.
grammar.commonMistake: Both subjects are sometimes kept, which produces "The cat which it caught the mouse" and leaves one word too many.
grammar.memoryTip: Swap the repeated subject for the pronoun. If you can still hear it or she sitting in the middle, delete the spare word.
grammar.practice:
Part A: Combine six pairs into single sentences: the boy and the race he trains for; the house that stands on the hill; the teacher who teaches maths; the river that flows through our town; the man in the blue jacket; the legend told by the elders. Part B: Read each new sentence aloud and check it still names the person or thing you mean. Part C: Combine two sentences of your own about the expedition in "The Hasty Route".

Answer key (self-check): Part A – model combinations (exact wording may vary; check that you used the right pronoun, placed the clause right after its noun, and did not double the subject): The boy who trains for the race arrives early every day. The house that stands on the hill is empty. The teacher who teaches maths is strict. The river that flows through our town is famous. The man who is wearing the blue jacket waved to us. The legend that is told by the elders explains the desert’s name. Part B – read each sentence aloud: it should still clearly name the boy, the house, the teacher, the river, the man and the legend, with nothing lost. Part C asks for “two sentences of your own,” so there is no single fixed answer – self-check by confirming your combined sentence keeps one subject and places the clause directly after its noun.

grammar.title: The No-Comma Rule for Defining Clauses
grammar.explanation: Defining relative clauses carry essential information, so no commas separate them from the rest of the sentence.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Correct: The boy who is wearing a red hat is my brother.
Incorrect: The boy, who is wearing a red hat, is my brother.
Correct: The girl who scored the goal celebrated with her team.
Correct: The storm that delayed us led to a well which had never been recorded before.
The commas in the incorrect version turn the clause into a different, non-defining kind that you will meet later. For now, defining means no commas.
grammar.commonMistake: Commas creep in out of habit, which shifts the meaning from "this particular boy" to "the boy, by the way, in a red hat".
grammar.memoryTip: Essential information needs no fence around it. If the clause could be lifted out with nothing lost, it was never defining.
grammar.practice:
Part A: Delete the unnecessary commas from four sentences and write out the corrected version. Part B: For one of them, explain how the meaning shifts once the commas go. Part C: Proofread your own legend for stray commas around defining clauses.

Answer key (self-check): the four target sentences for Part A are not listed in this exercise, so no fixed answer key can be given for Part A or Part B – self-check instead using the rule and the model already given: “The boy, who is wearing a red hat, is my brother” corrects to “The boy who is wearing a red hat is my brother,” and once the commas go the sentence returns to meaning “this particular boy” rather than an aside about him. Apply the same test to each of your four sentences: if the who/which/that clause is essential to knowing which person or thing is meant, it takes no commas. Part C checks “your own legend,” so self-check by scanning every who/which/that clause you wrote and confirming no commas surround it unless you truly intend a non-essential aside.

grammar.title: Four Common Mistakes and How to Repair Them
grammar.explanation: Four errors account for nearly every problem with defining relative clauses: extra commas, the wrong pronoun, the clause in the wrong place, and a doubled subject.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Mistake 1, commas: The girl, who scored the goal, celebrated. Repair: The girl who scored the goal celebrated.
Mistake 2, wrong pronoun: The book who I borrowed was interesting. Repair: The book which I borrowed was interesting.
Mistake 3, wrong position: Made the discovery the scientist won an award. Repair: The scientist who made the discovery won an award.
Mistake 4, doubled subject: The cat which it caught the mouse was fast. Repair: The cat which caught the mouse was fast.
grammar.commonMistake: Who is reached for automatically, so a book, a storm or a well ends up written about as though it were a person.
grammar.memoryTip: Ask one question before writing the pronoun: person or thing? People take who, things take which, and that covers both.
grammar.practice:
Part A: Repair four faulty sentences and name the mistake in each. Part B: Write one sentence containing each of the four errors, swap with a partner, and repair theirs. Part C: Explain to your partner why "The book who I borrowed" sounds wrong to an English ear.

Answer key: Part A – Mistake 1 (extra commas): “The girl, who scored the goal, celebrated.” → “The girl who scored the goal celebrated.” Mistake 2 (wrong pronoun): “The book who I borrowed was interesting.” → “The book which I borrowed was interesting.” Mistake 3 (wrong position): “Made the discovery the scientist won an award.” → “The scientist who made the discovery won an award.” Mistake 4 (doubled subject): “The cat which it caught the mouse was fast.” → “The cat which caught the mouse was fast.” Part C – who names people, and a book is a thing, so “who” must be replaced with “which” or “that.” Part B asks you to write your own sentence and swap with a partner, so there is no single fixed answer – self-check by confirming your four sentences each contain exactly one of the four mistakes above, then check any partner's repairs against the same four patterns.

grammar.title: Grade 5 Editing Focus: Future Plans, Comparatives, Opposites and Collocations
grammar.explanation: The unit's remaining language patterns are edited together: present continuous for arranged plans, comparative adjectives, opposites, and the verbs that pair naturally with particular nouns.
grammar.ruleAndExamples:
Present continuous for future plans uses am, is or are plus the -ing form with a future time phrase: We are documenting the site tomorrow. They are presenting the report next week. I am visiting the museum on Saturday.
Comparatives add -er to short adjectives and put more in front of long ones: hot becomes hotter, wise becomes wiser, reliable becomes more reliable, comfortable becomes more comfortable.
Opposites sharpen meaning: dreadful and delightful, miserable and prosperous, hasty and careful, reluctant and eager, grateful and irritable.
Collocations pair the natural verb with its noun: make a decision, face a challenge, share an experience, take a risk, reach a goal, make a discovery, achieve a result.
grammar.commonMistake: "More hotter" and "more wiser" compare twice over; a short adjective takes either the -er ending or more, never both together.
grammar.memoryTip: Count the syllables. One or two short syllables usually take -er, and three or more nearly always take more.
grammar.practice:
Part A: Rewrite three plans in the present continuous. We plan to explore the caves next Friday. She plans to meet the scientist on Monday. They plan to travel to the coast this weekend. Part C: Choose the natural verb for each noun: ___ a justifiable decision; ___ a dreadful outcome; ___ a delightful experience; ___ a remarkable discovery; ___ a profitable result. Part D: Compare Route A with Route B in two sentences, using three comparative adjectives.

Answer key: Part A – We are exploring the caves next Friday. She is meeting the scientist on Monday. They are travelling to the coast this weekend. Part B – dreadful → delightful; miserable → prosperous; hasty → careful; reluctant → eager; grateful → irritable. Part C – make a justifiable decision; face a dreadful outcome; share a delightful experience; make a remarkable discovery; achieve a profitable result. speaking.instructionsAndModelLines: Prepare and deliver a three-minute talk on what makes a tale timeless. Plan three points on cards, use at least six words from this unit, and finish with a question for your audience. Speak clearly, look up from your cards, and adjust your register if your listeners are younger than you. Model lines: "My first point is that oral tradition carried these tales for centuries before anyone wrote them down." "So here is my question for you: which story will your family still be telling in fifty years?"
speaking.aiTutorPrompt: Time my three-minute talk, count how many unit words I actually used, and suggest one change that would suit a younger audience.

writing.title: Writing 1: Write Your Own Legend
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write your own legend of 250 to 400 words. Plan first: choose a real place you know, a hero or heroine worth following, the quest or problem they face, one unlikely event, and the lesson the tale teaches. Organise it in three parts. The beginning introduces the setting, the hero and the quest, and opens with a classic phrase. The middle shows the hero facing difficulty, and includes description, at least two lines of dialogue and the unlikely event. The ending resolves the quest and states the moral. Work in at least two defining relative clauses and five words from this unit, then read the draft aloud before you hand it in.
writing.modelText: Long ago, in the hills above a fishing town, there lived a boy named Theo who could hear a storm three days before it arrived. One autumn the boats stopped returning, and the harbour master called the loss intolerable. Theo set off along the cliff path that nobody used, carrying only a lamp and a rope.
writing.sentenceStarter: Long ago, in the days when...
writing.expectedLength: 250 to 400 words in three clear parts

items: Plan – Place: the old well at Desert Point 4, out on the Adrar Plateau
Plan – Hero: a trader's daughter named Salma, known through the camp as reliable and honourable in every promise she made
Plan – Quest: bring back the caravan bell that fell down the well shaft two generations ago, so the villagers stop believing the well is cursed
Plan – Unlikely event: the rope lowering her into the shaft is worn thin and should not hold, yet it stops her exactly where the shaft narrows, no further and no less
Plan – Moral: a promise kept quietly is worth more than a promise made loudly

Beginning (classic phrase, setting, hero, quest): In ancient times, beside a well on the Adrar Plateau, there lived a trader's daughter named Salma, known through the camp as reliable and honourable in every promise she made. When the elders said the well was cursed because a caravan bell had vanished down its shaft two generations before, Salma promised she would bring it back into the light.

Middle (difficulty, description, two lines of dialogue, the unlikely event): The shaft that dropped away beneath the well's stone rim was narrower than her shoulders and darker than a moonless sky, and the climb down was dreadful even to imagine. "You do not have to do this," her uncle warned, gripping the old rope. "I gave my word," Salma answered, "and a faithful promise is not one you break when the dark gets deep." She tied the rope about her waist and was lowered down, expecting to fall forever — yet the rope, worn as it was, stopped her exactly where the shaft narrowed, as if it had been waiting for her all along.

Ending (resolves the quest, states the moral): Her fingers found the bell wedged in a crack of stone, and when she rang it once, the sound rolled out across the whole plateau. The villagers, grateful beyond words, called it a remarkable find, and the elders carved one line beside the rim: a promise kept quietly is worth more than a promise made loudly.
otherAnswers: Any real place, hero, quest, unlikely event and moral work equally well — for example a lighthouse keeper's son searching a flooded cave for a missing bell instead of a well on a desert plateau.
The moral can be worded differently as long as it teaches the same kind of lesson, such as: quiet loyalty outlasts a loud promise.

writing.successCriteria: I planned setting, hero, quest, unlikely event and moral; I opened with a classic phrase; I used at least two defining relative clauses with no commas; I used at least five unit words; I included two lines of dialogue; I stated the lesson at the end
writing.support: Fill in the five planning boxes before drafting, and borrow the shape of the legend of the Whispering Dunes for your three parts.
writing.extension: Add a second unlikely event that nearly defeats the hero, and vary your sentence openers so no two paragraphs begin the same way.

writing.title: Writing 2: Myth or Legend, and How to Tell
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write an explanation for a younger reader that sets out the difference between a myth and a legend. Give each form its own paragraph, name three features of it, and finish with a short paragraph on what the two forms share. Use an example of each: a myth that explains something in nature, and a legend built around a real place. Keep your tone helpful rather than showy, and define any word a younger reader might not know.
writing.modelText: A myth explains something people once found puzzling. Ancient listeners wanted to know why thunder rolled, so a myth gave the thunder a voice and a temper. A legend is different, because it begins with something real.
writing.sentenceStarter: The quickest way to tell a myth from a legend is...

items: Paragraph 1 (myth: definition, three features, example, defined word): A myth is an ancient story that explains something in nature — for example, a myth might explain why thunder rolls across the sky by saying a giant is angry up in the clouds. A myth has three main features: it is not based on fact, it includes gods, spirits or beings with powers no real person has, and it is set in a vague, timeless past that often opens with the words "Long, long ago". (Timeless here means it does not belong to any exact year in history.)

Paragraph 2 (legend: definition, three features, example, defined word): A legend is different, because it grows out of a real place, a real period of history, or a person who may once have lived. A legend I know tells of a hidden spring beneath the Whispering Dunes, sand hills on the edge of a real desert. A legend has three main features too: it follows a hero or heroine on a quest, storytellers add unlikely details until the tale grows far larger than the truth, and it ends by teaching something about a quality such as courage or patience. (A quest means a long, difficult journey to find or achieve something important.)

Paragraph 3 (what the two forms share): Even so, a myth and a legend share a great deal. Both travelled by oral tradition, which means people spoke them aloud long before anyone wrote them down, and both carry vivid description and a moral for the listener to carry away.
otherAnswers: Any myth that explains a natural event works just as well, such as one explaining why the sea tastes salty instead of why thunder rolls.
Any legend built around a real place or a real period of history is fine, such as a legend about an old bridge or a famous mountain path, instead of the Whispering Dunes.

writing.successCriteria: I gave each form its own paragraph; I named three features of each; I gave one example of each; I explained what they share; I defined the difficult words for a younger reader
writing.support: Use the feature lists from the information text as your bullet plan, and turn each bullet into one sentence.
writing.extension: Add a fourth paragraph on a tale that mixes features of both, and justify why it is hard to classify.

writing.title: Writing 3: The Moral of the Hasty Route
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a connected paragraph arguing whether the moral of "The Hasty Route" is proved by the story. Open with a topic sentence that states your view, support it with two quotations from parts 1 to 3, and explain what each quotation shows. Close by saying what a reader should take away. Use because, although and however to link your ideas rather than starting every sentence with a name.
writing.modelText: The story proves its moral, because the discovery arrives only after the team refuses to hurry. When Amal says "That is a reasonable idea if the weather holds", she weighs the risk instead of dismissing it.
writing.sentenceStarter: The story proves its moral, because...
writing.expectedLength: One developed paragraph with two quotations

items: Topic sentence stating the view: The story proves its moral, because every gain the team makes comes only after they slow down and think, never after they rush.

First quotation and explanation: This is shown when Amal says, "That is a reasonable idea if the weather holds," because she is weighing the guide's sandstorm warning instead of dismissing Noah's shortcut outright, and it is her caution that keeps the team safe once the storm arrives.

Second quotation and explanation, linked with because/although/however: It is proved again when Noah admits, "I was too forceful in my choice. Amal's slower plan was wiser," because although he wanted to save time at the start, however patient thinking was what led the team to the ancient well and the remarkable discovery of Desert Point 4.
Closing sentence on what a reader should take away: A reader should take away that patience is not the opposite of adventure; in this story, it is what makes the adventure possible.

writing.successCriteria: I began with a clear topic sentence; I quoted the story twice and punctuated the quotations; I explained what each quotation shows; I linked ideas with because, although or however; I finished with what the reader should take away
writing.support: Choose your two quotations first and write them out, then build the sentences around them.
writing.extension: Add a sentence that considers the opposite view, then explain why the evidence still favours yours.

writing.title: Writing 4: An Information Text on Oral Tradition
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Write a short information text for the class library explaining oral tradition: what it means, why stories travelled by voice, how storytellers remembered so much, and what changes when a tale is finally written down. Give the piece a heading and three subheadings, keep an impersonal style, and use at least three unit words accurately. Do not tell a story here; the purpose is to inform.
writing.modelText: Oral tradition means passing a story on by speaking it aloud. Before writing was widespread, a community's history, laws and warnings all travelled in this way, carried by people who had memorised them word for word.
writing.expectedLength: One heading, three subheadings and a paragraph under each

items: Heading: Oral Tradition: How Stories Travelled Before Writing

Subheading 1 — What Oral Tradition Means and Why It Travelled by Voice: Oral tradition means passing a story, a law or a piece of history on by speaking it aloud rather than by writing it down. Before writing was widespread, speech was the only reliable way a community could pass its knowledge to the next generation, so a storyteller's voice carried a remarkable amount of a group's history and laws.

Subheading 2 — How Storytellers Remembered So Much: Storytellers used patterns to hold a long tale in memory, including repeated phrases, rhythm, and a fixed order of events that never changed from one telling to the next. These patterns worked like a map through the story, so a single missed line did not collapse the whole telling.

Subheading 3 — What Changes When a Tale Is Written Down: Once a tale is written down, it stops changing from teller to teller and becomes a single fixed version that anyone can check word for word. This is part of the same phenomenon as the myths and legends studied in this unit: a written tale can no longer grow the unlikely details that a live storyteller once added.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote a heading and three subheadings; I kept an impersonal, factual style; I answered all four questions in the prompt; I used three unit words correctly; I checked that no sentence tells a story instead of informing
writing.support: Turn each of the four prompt questions into one subheading, then answer it in three sentences.
writing.extension: Add a short glossary of three terms, laid out as a bulleted list, and explain why each one matters.

writing.title: Writing 5: Reflect and Improve Your Legend
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Return to the legend you wrote in Writing 1 and improve it in three passes. Pass one: check the shape, and mark where the beginning, middle and ending start. Pass two: check the language, and replace three flat adjectives with precise unit words. Pass three: proofread for spelling, speech punctuation and stray commas around defining clauses. Then write four sentences explaining what you changed and why the legend now reads better.
writing.modelText: In my first draft the hero simply found the cave. I changed it to "the cave that had swallowed three lanterns", because the defining clause tells the reader why this cave matters and builds a little dread.
writing.sentenceStarter: The biggest improvement I made was...
writing.expectedLength: A revised legend plus four sentences of reflection

items: Pass one (mark the three parts): I drew a line before "In ancient times" to mark the beginning, before "The shaft that dropped away" to mark the middle, and before "Her fingers found the bell" to mark the ending.

Pass two (replace three flat adjectives with precise unit words): I changed "a good trader's daughter" to "a reliable trader's daughter", "a bad shaft" to "a dreadful shaft", and "a nice find" to "a remarkable find".

Pass three (proofread spelling, speech punctuation, stray commas): I corrected "caried" to "carried", moved the comma that had crept inside a defining clause in "the rope, that lowered her" back out to read "the rope that lowered her", and added the closing quotation mark I had missed after Salma's line "I gave my word".
Reflection sentence 1: I changed "a good trader's daughter" to "a reliable trader's daughter" because good tells the reader nothing specific about Salma's character.
Reflection sentence 2: I changed "a bad shaft" to "a dreadful shaft" because dreadful matches the fear Salma feels as she is lowered into the dark.
Reflection sentence 3: I changed "a nice find" to "a remarkable find" because remarkable shows how rare and important the bell really was.

Reflection sentence 4: Removing the comma from the defining clause mattered most, because without it the sentence briefly suggested there was only one rope in the world rather than picking out the one rope that mattered here.

writing.successCriteria: I marked the three parts of my legend; I replaced three flat adjectives with precise unit words; I proofread speech punctuation and commas; I explained four changes; I said why each change improved the piece
writing.support: Work with a partner and read each other's legends aloud, because the ear catches what the eye skips.
writing.extension: Rewrite your weakest paragraph twice in different ways, then explain which version you kept and why.

writing.title: Writing 6: Retell a Scene from Noah's Viewpoint
writing.origin: Ehel English Content Template v1.2 curriculum expansion
writing.promptAndInstructions: Rewrite the sandstorm scene from part 1 of "The Hasty Route" as Noah would tell it, in the first person. Show what he notices, what he feels as the wind rises, and how he judges his own advice afterwards. Keep every event of the original scene, but change nothing about the facts. Use at least two defining relative clauses and two words from the feelings group.
writing.modelText: I was the one who wanted to press on, and I still remember the moment the light changed. The ridge that Amal had chosen suddenly seemed like the safest ground in Mauritania.
writing.expectedLength: Two paragraphs in the first person

items: Paragraph 1 (notices, feelings as things build): I was the one who wanted to press on past the first stop, and I still remember insisting to Amal that we were only slowing ourselves down. She studied the clouds instead of arguing back, and I told her I was not reluctant to take risks, though part of me already felt anxious about the strange colour of the sky. By noon we reached the ridge that Amal had chosen, where the air turned cooler and surprisingly pleasant, and we sat down to eat lunch under a large rock. Leo said he was grateful we had packed shade cloths, and Daniel added that he was grateful he had listened to Amal, because our side of the ridge was cooler than the other — and hearing that, I said nothing at all.

Paragraph 2 (the storm, feelings, judging his own advice): Then a loud sound rolled across the dunes, a wind that grew fast and heavy within moments. "It is a sandstorm!" I shouted, and we scrambled to cover the supplies and crouched under the cloths while the sand hit us like needles. Leo coughed and called it dreadful, saying we should have stayed at camp, but Amal simply said we needed to wait it out — and crouched there in the stinging wind, I judged my own advice honestly for the first time: the shortcut I had pushed for would have left us with no shelter and no ridge to hide behind.

writing.successCriteria: I wrote in the first person as Noah; I kept every event of the original scene; I showed his feelings rather than listing them; I used two defining relative clauses; I used two words from the feelings group
writing.support: List the five events of the scene in order first, then write one or two sentences for each.
writing.extension: Add a closing sentence in which Noah judges his own advice honestly, using a word from the judgement group.

assignments.title: Telling Timeless Tales portfolio: an original legend and a retelling
assignments.instructions: Submit two pieces. Second, a recording of the retelling from Speaking 1, opening with a classic phrase, changing voice for each character and closing on the moral. Marking: 16 marks for the legend using the writing rubric, and 16 marks for the recording using the speaking rubric. teacherNotes.note: Pre-teach myth, legend, oral tradition, quest and phenomenon before the information text, because the whole unit rests on those five ideas. Several learners will meet twenty-five adjectives at once, so introduce one vocabulary group per session rather than the full list. An adult must sit with the learner for every AI tutor task and every recording; a child is never left alone with the device, and recordings stay inside the class space. Give feedback on quoting accurately, on placing the relative clause straight after its noun, and on avoiding commas inside a defining clause. Some children have lived through severe weather, so introduce the sandstorm scene gently and let anyone step out of the discussion.

teacherNotes.noteType: Grammar answer key and AI tutor guidance
teacherNotes.note:
Grammar answers, teacher copy. Grammar 2 Part A: that or which, which or that, who or that, which or that, who or that, that or which. Grammar 3 Part A: The boy who trains every morning won the race. The house that stands on the hill is very old. The teacher who teaches us maths is strict but fair. The river which flows through our town is very wide. The man who was wearing a blue jacket helped us find the way. The legend that was told by the elders teaches us about patience. Grammar 5 Part A: remove the commas; change who to which or that; move the clause after the noun; delete the doubled subject it. Grammar 6 Part A: We are exploring the caves next Friday. She is meeting the scientist on Monday. They are travelling to the coast this weekend. Part B: delightful, prosperous, careful, eager, irritable. Part C: make, face, share, make, achieve.
Tutor guidance. Steer learners towards asking the tutor to check a clause they have already written rather than to write one for them, and towards asking for a further example when a rule has not landed. Remind the class that the tutor is a practice partner, not a marker, and that every session happens with an adult in the room.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Model sort. Positive feelings or qualities: grateful, pleasant, delightful, glorious, remarkable, significant, prosperous. Negative: furious, anxious, irritable, miserable, dreadful, intolerable. Character and behaviour: forceful, dutiful, honourable, reliable, contagious, hasty. Judgement or possibility: imaginable, justifiable, profitable, reasonable, mysterious, reluctant. Accept any other placement the learner justifies in writing; hasty, contagious and mysterious are the three that most often move column.

Pairs: dreadful and delightful; prosperous and miserable; reluctant and eager; grateful and irritable; pleasant and intolerable. Award the second mark only where the sentence holds both words of the pair and the contrast is visible, for example "The morning was pleasant, but the afternoon heat became intolerable."

Gaps: (1) pleasant, (2) anxious, (3) dreadful, (4) miserable, (5) reliable, (6) reasonable, (7) remarkable, (8) profitable. Accept glorious for (1), intolerable for (4) and significant for (7) where the paragraph still reads sensibly. Reject any answer that breaks the grammar, such as an adverb in gap 5.

Look for ten different words, each in an original sentence tied to myths, legends or adventure, with the word doing real work rather than being dropped in. At least one sentence must be a question and one must be dialogue with speech marks. Mark the suffix spelling closely: -able and -ible are the usual slips.

Groups. -ful: grateful, dreadful, delightful, forceful, dutiful. -ous: furious, mysterious, glorious, contagious, anxious, prosperous. -able or -ible: imaginable, justifiable, profitable, reasonable, intolerable, reliable, honourable, miserable, remarkable. -ant: pleasant, reluctant, significant. Accept faithful, joyous, sensible and important as added words. The spelling note should mention dropping the final e before -able, as in desire and desirable.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: Expected finds. Defining clauses: "the explorers who found Desert Point 4" (part 3), "the decisions that taught them patience" (part 3), "a well which had never been recorded before" (part 3), "the wells that supplied the village" (the legend). Present continuous plans: "We are documenting the full route tomorrow" (part 1) and "We are presenting the full trail report to the science club next week" (part 2). Legend feature: the hidden spring showing itself only to a patient traveller is the unlikely event.

answerKey.answerOrGuidance: hasty. It names speed without thought; glorious describes beauty, contagious describes spreading, and reasonable describes a sensible judgement.
reluctant. The other three options describe wealth, something extraordinary and something important, none of which is about hesitation.
which. Who is for people, whoever is not a relative pronoun in this pattern, and when introduces a time rather than a thing.
The boy who is wearing a red hat is my brother. The other three all insert at least one comma, which turns the clause into the non-defining kind.
oral. The information text defines oral tradition as speaking a tale aloud long before anyone writes it down.
pleasant. The ridge has just been described as cooler, so the missing adjective must be positive; the other three are all negative.
justifiable. Amal calls the shortcut fair and understandable, and immediately explains it by saying Noah wanted to save time.
more reliable. Reliable has four syllables, so it takes more; most would compare three or more things, and reliabler is not a word.
We are exploring the caves next Friday. The present continuous plus the future time phrase next Friday shows a plan already arranged.
make. English says make a discovery and make a decision; challenge takes face, goal takes reach, and risk takes take.

grownUpGuide.label: Teacher & Parent Guide
grownUpGuide.intro: In this unit, your child works through "Telling Timeless Tales" on their own — new words, a grammar focus, and a set of longer readings. This guide shows you what they are working on so you can talk about it with them.

sections.title: 🧭 About this unit (please read first)
sections.body:
Your child is about 9-10 years old and works through this unit largely on their own — reading, practising and checking answers at their own pace. Your role is different from the early grades: you keep them company from outside the screen rather than leading each page.

The most useful things you can do are also the simplest: ask what the unit's texts are about, listen to them read a paragraph aloud, hear the new words used in sentences, and read their writing when they submit it. A few minutes of real conversation about the unit turns silent screen work into language they can actually use.

This guide tells you what the unit covers so you can ask good questions without working through the pages yourself.

sections.title: 💬 Using the AI Tutor with your child
sections.body:
At this age your child can use the AI Tutor on their own — it is worth sitting in occasionally to see how they use it, and showing them what it can do.

Suggest they ask it to quiz them on this unit's words: "Ask me questions about the word 'hasty'."

Suggest they paste in a sentence of their own and ask whether it sounds natural, and how to say it better.

Encourage 'why' questions — why a comma goes there, why the text says it that way. Asking the tutor to explain, not just to check, is where the learning is.

sections.title: 🌟 Tips for supporting this unit
sections.body:
Short, regular sessions still beat one long one. A unit spread over several days sticks; a unit crammed in one sitting does not.

Talk about the reading away from the screen — over a meal, in the car. Retelling a text in their own words is one of the strongest checks of understanding there is.

Treat their writing as a draft to improve, not an answer to mark. Pick one thing to praise and one thing to sharpen, and stop there.

Praise precision and persistence, not just speed. At this stage careful, complete answers matter more than quick ones.

sections.title: What Your Child Will Be Able to Do
items: Explain the difference between a myth and a legend.
Identify the key features of classic tales: oral tradition, timeless settings, moral or explanatory purpose, and larger-than-life characters.
Use defining relative clauses to add essential information to your sentences.
Use the present continuous tense to talk about future plans and arrangements.
Compare things using comparative adjectives (e.g., more reliable, hotter, wiser).
Identify and use opposites (antonyms) such as dreadful/delightful and miserable/prosperous.
Match verbs with nouns correctly in collocations (e.g., make a decision, face an outcome).
Write your own short legend with a clear beginning, middle and end.

sections.title: How to Support This Unit, Step by Step
sections.body:
A simple shape for staying involved without taking over:

1. Before they start (2 min)
Skim this guide's word list and text titles so you know what to ask about later. You do not need to work through the pages yourself.

2. While they work
Let them work alone at their own pace. Be within reach for a word or an instruction they cannot crack, but resist doing the thinking for them.

3. Talk about the reading (5 min)
Ask them to tell you what "Myths and Legends: What Makes a Tale Timeless" was about in their own words, and what happened in "The Hasty Route, part 1" — and what they thought of it.

4. Hear the words (5 min)
Pick a few words from the list below and ask for each one in a spoken sentence of their own. Saying a word out loud fixes it far better than reading it silently.

5. Check the grammar landed (3 min)
Ask them to explain "What a Defining Relative Clause Does" to you as if you were the student. Teaching it back is the quickest way to find out whether it stuck.

6. Read their writing (5 min)
When the Writing section is submitted, read it together. Praise one specific thing, suggest one improvement, and leave it there.

sections.title: Simple Check — What to Look For
sections.body: You do not need a test. These are the signs the unit has landed — listen for them in conversation and look for them in the writing:
items: Comprehension items 1, 6 and 11 sorted correctly, plus a one-minute spoken explanation in Speaking 5.
Four features of a classic tale listed and matched to lines from the legend in Activities 6.
Six correct relative pronouns in Grammar 2 and two accurate defining clauses inside the learner's own legend.
Three plans rewritten in the present continuous in Grammar 6 Part A, with the future time phrase kept.
Route A and Route B compared in two sentences using three correctly formed comparative adjectives.
Five opposite pairs matched in Activities 2 and each pair used in one sentence.
Five verb-noun collocations completed in Grammar 6 Part C with no verb repeated wrongly.
An original legend of 250 to 400 words with a hero, a quest, an unlikely event, two defining clauses and a stated moral.
